ideas.idea: The textbook already concedes that under uncertainty planning and control move toward where work is done, direction-only planning suits uncertain levels, and complex change needs employee involvement, so the quarrel is with the playbook more than the theory.
A cascaded KPI is a task; tasks go stale when the situation changes while the intent behind them endures, so intent is predominant.
Attach a stated purpose ('in order to…') to every cascaded target and let the purpose govern when the number goes stale.
Replace detailed target cascades with commander's intent and let teams choose the how.
Mission tactics: prescribe method only as far as coordination needs; subordinates act on initiative and inform rather than wait for permission; seniors intervene by exception.
Under uncertainty precise central control is impossible, and the further ahead a plan looks the less precision it should impose.
Information technology and live dashboards tempt seniors to keep precise, positive control over subordinates, which the doctrine calls incompatible with its command philosophy.
People should understand intent two levels up; test whether someone two levels down can state why their targets exist.
Name a single main effort and treat everything else as secondary, with economy elsewhere, instead of many equally weighted KPIs.
Decentralised initiative needs a unifying focus or it dissipates strength; mission command is not licence to do as one likes.
The textbook's evidence that specific, difficult goals raise performance is real (Weyerhaeuser log trucks).
Keep plain targets on stable, routine work; the contradictions bite on uncertain work.
ideas.note: textbook places goal planning in the low-uncertainty technical core

ideas.idea: Schedule or target pressure makes organisations accept risk in small, unseen increments: Columbia's programmes were judged by days of margin to one launch date.
A run of success normalises deviance: past success is taken as evidence of safety, so a good quarter or clean record is not proof of control.
In quarterly reviews ask what nearly went wrong or which deviation you got away with, not only whether the target was hit.
For every target ask what people will stop doing to hit it, and track that hidden cost too.
Production behaviours win over prevention unless leaders actively reinforce prevention; schedule makes efficiency a strong signal and safety a weak one.
Things get counted because they can be; results are lagging indicators; measure what matters, not what is easy.
Grading performance with charts in a review stifles discussion; measure, but do not grade in the room where you need the truth.
These traditions are not anti-planning or anti-metrics: schedules are essential, aggressive schedules can signal health, and DOE tracks metrics on whether fixes worked.
Separate those who own cost and schedule from those who can say stop on quality or risk (an independent technical authority).
NASA inverted the burden of proof, making engineers prove a flight unsafe rather than proving it safe.
Flip the burden of proof in go/no-go and forecast reviews: 'prove to me it has not been harmed'.
Information is rolled up and simplified as it rises, weak signals drop out, and the steering committee hears a filtered green story.
Leaders facing unanimity should argue the other side, seek dissent or designate a devil's advocate.
Consensus sign-off verified by everyone's signature renders no one accountable; each decision needs an owner.
Subordinates owe honest disagreement before a decision and full support after; yes-men are not tolerated.
Performance is mostly a property of the system: error is a symptom of system failure, so ask how the organisation failed the individual rather than how the individual failed.
Roughly 85% or more of event causes are organisational and perhaps 90% of unsafe acts are blameless.
ideas.note: D restates it as 'over 90% of errors organisationally induced', a conflation

ideas.idea: 81% of causal factors are latent organisational weaknesses and 19% active worker errors.
ideas.note: DOE gives a 70/30 split of human error (vol1:1191) and 81% for design problems in engineer events (vol1:1247); no 81/19 split

ideas.idea: Blame drives error reports underground: a review that scores people teaches them to hide mistakes, and a just culture is a prerequisite for a reporting culture.
Firewall learning reviews from appraisal and pay, with a written promise that what is said there will not be used against people.
Replace top-down critiques and debriefs with participant-led, rank-free after-action reviews after major events.
An AAR is not a critique: it does not grade success or failure and sets rank aside.
Accountability is redefined as giving an honest account (forward-looking), not as punishment.
Apply the substitution test: would comparable peers have done the same in the same situation?
Judge decisions on what was known at the time, not on how they turned out; outcome-scored reviews punish the bold miss and reward the safe non-attempt.
The Marines treat errors of overboldness leniently and inaction or timidity severely, with no zero-defects mentality.
A review should ask whether the person ducked a decision that was theirs to make, not only whether results came in.
Sources split on speed: the Marines say any decision beats none, while DOE and Columbia require proof of safety before proceeding.
Sources split on rules versus judgement: DOE demands rigorous procedure regardless of perceived risk, MCDP1 is non-prescriptive, and Columbia holds both.
Sources split on oversight: Columbia wants independent technical authority over programme managers, while MCDP1 keeps authority with the line commander and DOE with line management.
Sort decisions by reversibility or consequence: prove-it-safe for the irreversible few (cash, data, compliance, safety), act fast on the reversible many (pricing, sales, product bets).
ideas.note: no source frames the split by reversibility; follows from MCDP1 versus DOE/CAIB contexts

ideas.idea: Columbia names the ability to operate centrally or decentrally as appropriate as the hallmark of a high-reliability organisation.
Sources split on causes: DOE keeps root-cause analysis, while the wildfire guide bars causal statements and uses networked causality.
Recommendations can interfere with learning: they add complexity that raises risk, and managers jump to an action plan and think the problem solved.
Structural changes add complexity and new ways to fail, and error risk rises at first as old and new ways compete.
Audit past action items for how many added process versus removed it, and stop adding a committee for every lesson.
Use root-cause fixes for patterns, process and equipment failures, and reconstruct the conditions for single incidents and judgement calls.
ideas.note: J notes the same split inside the wildfire guide

ideas.idea: Sources split on how blameless: NHS and DOE decision trees keep discipline for some cases, the wildfire guide sets the bar at reckless and wilful disregard, and the Marines give no licence for recklessness.
Sources split on retraining: the Army retrains to standard, DOE calls retraining for slips a waste and an insult, and the wildfire guide counts forced retraining as discipline.
Sources split on standards: the Army AAR judges against fixed standards, while the wildfire guide cautions against judging events by broken rules.
Columbia held that problems are not solved by retirements, resignations or transfers, and kept witness statements privileged, apart from personal accountability.
Leaders create culture and must change it, so the work sits with the executive team, not the change programme.
Put the senior team's and steering committee's own decisions under review; learning reviews seldom examine the officials who commissioned them.
Counting delivered changes breeds a false belief the problem is solved; post-Challenger fixes became the next blind spot.
Treat a steering committee as a temporary advisory group whose need depends on the size of the change.
Repurpose the steering committee to hunt bad news and fund fixes rather than collect green reports or police people; judge it by whether bad news arrives faster.
DOE's steering committee that tracks accountability clashes with the learning-review insistence on separating reviews from management oversight.
ideas.note: firewall is against administrative action against employees, not against oversight committees

ideas.idea: Kotter's top-down model fits predictable change; the more complex the change, the more employees need a hand in planning it.
New rules coming out of a review should be vetted by the people who do the work before adoption.
Defer to expertise: move decision authority to those closest to the work.
Approval loops and committee sign-off run slower than events; excessive control slows tempo.
ideas.note: C's 'slowing execution to a crawl' adds strength

ideas.idea: Executives cannot see the gap between work as imagined and work as done; surface it.
Practical drift: experience teaches which rules can be shortcut, so answering failure with more rules or compliance is naive.
Map feedback loops and delays before a change programme; linear interventions provoke counter-intuitive system responses.
ideas.note: 'policy resistance' term is not in the library

ideas.idea: Frontline intuition (MCDP1) clashes with systems mapping, which says intuition fails on accumulations and delays.
Organise cross-functional teams with broad mandates instead of functional silos run for resource utilisation, which breed local optimisation.
ideas.note: D's claim that Org Topologies blames goal cascading is not in the source

ideas.idea: Agile's flat self-managing teams clash with an independent technical authority parallel to programme management.
Fixed sprints clash with continuous flow; Kanban and Reinertsen say timeboxes impose artificial batching.
ideas.note: library has batch size and WIP; no source argues timeboxes impose batching; Reinertsen absent

ideas.idea: Limit work in progress at executive level; smaller batches speed feedback.
High Reliability Theory and Normal Accident Theory disagree on whether failure can be engineered out; DOE is the more optimistic.
Who owns improvement splits: DOE relies on a management champion, Scrum gives it to the team.
Track a handful of useful KPIs, not a laundry list.
Target pressure quietly alters the criteria so work can still be certified, rather than prompting open cheating.
Following the process is not the same as being safe: allegiance to hierarchy, procedure and proper channels silenced engineering warnings.
Sources split on purpose: DOE makes safe work the overriding priority, while the Forest Service says it exists to do its mission, not to be safe, so a company is not a nuclear plant.
Treat routine managerial changes as error risks; most daily management involves some change.
DOE itself lists ignoring other industries' operating experience as an at-risk practice.
At about 300 people executives lose direct line of sight and middle layers filter what reaches them.
At 300 people a shared philosophy and familiarity are still achievable, making decentralisation less risky.
ideas.note: MCDP1 ties decentralisation to familiarity and trust (mcdp1-warfighting.md:2540); size claim is the answer's

ideas.idea: A subordinate without a clear purpose should ask for one; a missing intent is a leadership failure.
Columbia: 'NASA's blind spot is it believes it has a strong safety culture.'
The textbook's expectancy theory ties reward to individual results, against the sources' system view.
The textbook itself records doubts about appraisal: GE and others dropped forced ranking, and 58% of executives say performance management drives neither engagement nor performance.
The textbook treats inappropriate goals and behaviour as fixable control-system faults; Columbia treats them as how the accident happened.
The top is last to see target pressure: NASA management denied schedule pressure that the workforce felt.
Where status is missing, numbers are the great equaliser, so data gives a voice without rank its weight.
Critiques should dwell on why something was done and why it produced its result, not only on what was done.
